title: Comparing the Value Relevance of Two Operating Income Measures

models.model_label: Valuation regression with STREET operating income (Eq. 1, Table 2, all three groups combined)
models.sample_description: Firm-quarter observations in 1989–1997 where STREET and EPSOP differ, with all three disagreement groups combined. Group membership is based on how EPSOP and STREET compare with GAAP earnings from continuing operations (Compustat Q19). Each observation requires I/B/E/S and Compustat data; cases where STREET and EPSOP agree are omitted.
models.method_details: The authors identify Eq. (1) as a valuation regression but do not name its underlying estimator; it is not inferred.
models.equation_text: P_{i,t} = βV0 + βV1 BV_{i,t} + βV2 OPINC_{i,t} + βV3 (NI_{i,t} − OPINC_{i,t}) + ε_{i,t}

fixed_effects.details: No fixed-effects setting is reported for Eq. (1).

standard_errors.details: The paper reports cross-equation slope t-tests and adjusted-R-squared Vuong tests, but does not specify a standard-error correction or clustering for Eq. (1).

evidence.quote: Pi;t 1⁄4 bV0 þ bV1BVi;t þ bV2OPINCi;t þ bV3ðNI - OPINCÞi;t þ ei;t; ð1Þ

estimation_procedure.description: Eq. (1) is estimated on all three disagreement groups combined, using STREET as the operating-income measure. The authors compare the separate STREET and EPSOP equations using a Vuong test for adjusted R-squared and a t-test for the OPINC slope; the slope-difference t-value uses the stated unequal-variance approximation.

evidence.quote: We use a Vuong test to determine whether one valuation equation has a significantly larger adjusted-R-square.
We also compare coefficient estimates on the OPINC variable and use a t-test to determine whether one operating income measure has a larger coefficient in the valuation equation.
we estimate the t-value by dividing the difference between the two coefficient estimates by the square root of the summation of the variances of the two coefficient estimates.

other.description: The paired valuation comparison uses a Vuong test for adjusted R-squared and a t-test for the difference in OPINC slopes, with the t-value calculated using the unequal-variance approximation described in note 12.

evidence.quote: We use a Vuong test to determine whether one valuation equation has a significantly larger adjusted-R-square.

we estimate the t-value by dividing the difference between the two coefficient estimates by the square root of the summation of the variances of the two coefficient estimates.

review_notes: The selected result is the full-sample all-three-groups-combined comparison; group-specific valuations are follow-up partitions. The STREET and EPSOP regressions are separate co-primary measurement proxies for the paper’s stated comparison.

models.model_label: Three-day information-content regression with STREET (Eq. 2, Table 3, all three groups combined)
models.sample_description: Firm-quarter observations in 1989–1997 where STREET and EPSOP differ, with all three disagreement groups combined. Group membership is based on how EPSOP and STREET compare with GAAP earnings from continuing operations (Compustat Q19). Each observation requires I/B/E/S and Compustat data, plus CRSP data for the information-content regression; cases where STREET and EPSOP agree are omitted.
models.method_details: The information-content methodology explicitly describes OLS regression.

fixed_effects.details: No fixed-effects setting is reported for Eq. (2).

standard_errors.details: The paper reports proxy-slope t-tests and adjusted-R-squared Vuong tests, but does not state a regression standard-error correction or clustering.

evidence.quote: CARi;t 1⁄4 bIC0 þ bIC1UOPINCi;t þ ei;t; ð2Þ

estimation_procedure.description: OLS regression of three-day market-adjusted CAR on unexpected operating income using STREET. The authors estimate separate equations with STREET or EPSOP, compare adjusted R-squared by a Vuong test and compare slopes by t-test; the paper also estimates a 63-day replication, which is excluded from the selected baseline family.

evidence.quote: The measure with the most explanatory power in the OLS regression is considered to be the most value relevant.
We use a Vuong test to determine whether one specification has a significantly larger adjusted R-square and a t-test to determine whether one slope coefficient is significantly larger than the other.
we estimate the t-value by dividing the difference between the two coefficient estimates by the square root of the summation of the variances of the two coefficient estimates.

other.description: The paired information-content comparison uses a Vuong test for adjusted R-squared and a t-test for the difference in UOPINC slopes, using the unequal-variance approximation in note 12.

evidence.quote: We use a Vuong test to determine whether one specification has a significantly larger adjusted R-square and a t-test to determine whether one slope coefficient is significantly larger than the other.
we estimate the t-value by dividing the difference between the two coefficient estimates by the square root of the summation of the variances of the two coefficient estimates.

review_notes: The three-day window is the primary information-content specification. The 63-day window is explicitly introduced as a replication to mitigate timing concerns and is excluded as a sensitivity analysis.

missing_fields.dependent_variable.formula: The paper says CAR is market-adjusted but does not specify the exact benchmark return or adjustment calculation.

dependent_variable.name: CAR_i,t
dependent_variable.definition: Three-trading-day market-adjusted cumulative abnormal return around the quarterly earnings announcement: CRSP returns from days −1 through +1, with day 0 from the Compustat announcement date. The source does not provide the benchmark-return adjustment formula.

evidence.quote: CARi,t is the three-trading days or 63-trading days market-adjusted return for firm i for days - 1 to þ 1
CARi,t: Three trading day market-adjusted cumulative abnormal returns surrounding earnings announcement day 0.

independent_variables.name: UOPINC_i,t
independent_variables.definition: Unexpected operating income for quarter t using STREET: the selected STREET operating-income number minus the last mean consensus estimate in the I/B/E/S Summary file before the quarterly earnings announcement, divided by the share price at the beginning of the quarter.
independent_variables.formula: (STREET_i,t − last pre-announcement mean I/B/E/S consensus estimate_i,t) / beginning-of-quarter share price

evidence.quote: UOPINCit is the unexpected operating income for firm i in quarter t, defined as operating income minus expected operating income divided by the beginning of quarter share price.
UOPINCi,t: Unexpected operating income is defined as the difference between the operating income number and expected operating income, divided by the price per share at the beginning of the quarter.
The last mean consensus estimate in the I/B/E/S Summary file prior to the quarterly earnings announcement is our proxy for expected operating income.
The expected operating income number is the last mean consensus estimate from the I/B/E/S Summary file prior to the quarterly earnings announcement.
STREET: Operating income reported by Thomson Financial I/B/E/S.

result_sets.population: All three disagreement groups combined; N=22,092 firm-quarter observations.

samples.sample_label: Firm-quarters where I/B/E/S STREET and Compustat EPSOP differ (1989–1997)
samples.period_detail: Quarterly data; sample ends in 1997 because I/B/E/S operating earnings are required in primary EPS form.

sample_unit.quote:
Using quarterly data
from 1989 to 1997, we show that operating income provided by managers and
analysts is more value relevant than operating income obtained from 10-Q and 10-K
filings to the SEC under all three procedures.

sample_period.quote:
Our sample period begins in 1989 because EPSOP is
unavailable prior to 1988. It ends in 1997 because we require our data to be stated in
primary EPS

data_sources.quote:
we use Thomson Financial I/B/E/S data to measure operating income disclosed in a
firm’s earnings release (hereafter STREET).

We use Standard and Poor’s (S&P)
data to measure EPS from operations obtained from 10-Q and 10-K filings to the
SEC (Compustat item Q177, hereafter EPSOP).

We impose a CRSP data requirement only for
information content tests.

sample_extraction.data_section_full_text:
1. Sample


Each firm-quarter observation in our sample must have I/B/E/S and Compustat data.
We conduct predictive ability tests using a seasonal random walk (SRW) model (i.e.,
expected earnings in quarter t equal those in quarter t-4) so STREET and EPSOP must
be available in quarter t and t-4. We impose a CRSP data requirement only for
information content tests. Our sample period begins in 1989 because EPSOP is
unavailable prior to 1988. It ends in 1997 because we require our data to be stated in
primary EPS and beginning in 1998, most I/B/E/S data are stated as fully diluted EPS.

data_section_spans.end_anchor: primary EPS and beginning in 1998, most I/B/E/S data are stated as fully diluted EPS.
